comment: Keep plots 0 and 1 (Natural History and American History) exactly as they are. Fix plot 2, the National Museum of African American History and Culture: its corona reads as a stack of flat copper slabs, a generic tiered pagoda. The real corona is three tiers, each tier a tall band whose four walls lean OUTWARD as they rise (an inverted, stepped pyramid: each tier wider at its top than at its bottom, and each tier starting a little wider than the top of the one below), clad all over in a bronze lattice screen. Rebuild it so: a recessed dark glass base storey; then three tiers of about 4 blocks high each, every tier stepping out by 1 block per 2 courses on all four sides (use upside-down cut copper stairs on the outer faces so the walls read as leaning out), the top tier the widest, with a flat roof. Clad the tier walls in a uniform warm bronze lattice: waxed cut copper with a regular pattern of small dark openings (trapdoors or dark glass panes behind iron bars) over every face, glowing amber at dusk from lights behind the screen. Keep the porch canopy and reflecting pool on the south side, and the footprint.
summary: I rebuilt plot 2's corona in parts/roofs-corona.mjs and re-ran the build. It is now an inverted stepped pyramid of three leaning tiers, each 4 courses high (y8–11, 12–15, 16–19), clad in a bronze lattice with amber light behind it. The tiers sit over a dark glass base that is set back further than before, under a flat roof. I compared the result cell by cell with v1: plots 0 and 1 are unchanged (0 cells differ), and all changes are inside x188..214, y4..20, z0..26. The north, south and east views look right. Plot 2 has no floating or orphan blocks.
applied: Recessed dark glass base: the black-glass storey with copper mullions (y4..7) now sits at inset 6 (x194..208, z6..20), one cell inside tier 1's foot, so it reads as set back under the corona. To match, I moved the main glass doors from z21 to z20 in parts/glaze-light.mjs.

Three tiers about 4 blocks high, leaning out 1 block per 2 courses on all four sides: from bottom to top each tier's courses sit at insets 5,5,4,4 / 3,3,2,2 / 1,1,0,0. Each tier starts one block wider than the top of the one below, and the top tier is the widest, filling the footprint edge.
Upside-down waxed cut copper stairs run along the outer faces at every outward step, with top-half cut copper slabs at the corners, so the walls read as leaning rather than as flat slabs.
Uniform bronze lattice on every face: a checker of waxed cut copper and waxed copper grate. The grate cells are the regular small dark openings, and the cut copper corners are solid.
Amber glow at dusk: one cell behind the screen is a ring of brown stained glass with an ochre froglight about every 4th cell on every course, so light shows through the grate openings.

Flat roof: a smooth stone deck inside a cut copper slab coping ring at y20. Flush froglights in a 6-block grid keep the roof lit (lowest light level 2, no dark cells), and the inner ring of the top course is deck, not lights.
Kept the porch canopy, its posts, the reflecting pools, the entry walk, the grounds and the footprint as they were.
skipped: Iron bars behind the openings: I didn't add these. The person offered trapdoors or dark glass behind bars as one option, and at this scale a copper grate cell (a perforated bronze block with the amber glass behind it) gives the same small-opening look in one block, using blocks already in the palette.

Fitting all four requests inside the footprint: a 2-block lean per tier, a step out between tiers, a set-back base and a top tier that ends at the footprint edge need more width than the plot has. As the nearest fit, each tier leans out 1 block (half-steps shown by the stairs), steps out 1 more at each join, and the base moved in from inset 5 to 6 to make room.

Plots 0 and 1, as asked. The pre-existing check warnings there (orphan blocks on the Natural History roof and drum, dark cells at y20, the 'outlier' flag on the porch posts' deepslate walls) are from the earlier build, not this change, and I left them alone.
